chapter: Life in New York in the 1940s
title: Marijuana in New York: Mezz Mezzrow, reefer pads and sweet potato pie
summary: Edison recalls marijuana as common and tolerated in the 1930s-40s, buying joints in speakeasies and listening to records in the pads.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: When did that drug thing with heroin and everything sort of come on strong? In the '40s?

In the '40s. You know, Stanley, I remember New York when the marijuana was prevalent around there. The police never even bothered you most of the time because that's all it was. They knew it wasn't detrimental to anybody.
It was so common, I guess.

It was common in those days, you know. And as you know, Mezz Mezzrow, he was the man around New York, you know. And at that time everybody went by the apartment house where he used to live, 2040, you know, and it was just automatic that you'd knock on the door for a couple of joints, you know.

I met him when I first came here. And we went backstage at the Paramount where Lionel was with Benny Goodman. And Mezz used to have a 50 flat tin of Chesterfield cigarettes in his right pocket and then he had another tin, the same type, in this pocket, which was not Chesterfields.
(Laughter.)

Yeah. And it was a known fact that everybody did it, you know. And the police never bothered you. They used to have places in New York called the reefer pads, you know, called them pads in those days. And then if you smoked, they called you a viper. And we used to go to places, speakeasies, and we'd get a couple of joints for a quarter. And they would give you a little sliver of sweet potato pie, you know.
Why is that?
Well, you'd have a sweet taste after you smoked the joint. You want something sweet, you know. That's the reason why that Cab used to sing, 'If You're a Viper.'
remember that?
Yeah.
"Dream about a reefer five foot long."
And it was a popular record. But nowadays, they won't even let you mention that on a record. But in those days, you'd truck on down to the candy store, you know.
(Inaudible).
Candy, right.
You know, I didn't really -- I didn't really comprehend what that meant, you know.
Put the two together.
I thought that was another name but literally it was a craving for that?

Sure, it's your craving for something sweet. And oh, the places, you know -- New York was so great then. It was just a fantastic city. And everybody was so close together. And it was -- oh, they had many of those pads, had the red lights on, and you had all the good records playing for you, like the Billie Holiday records, the Louie Armstrong records. The big bands, Chick Webb, Ella Fitzgerald. Basie would be playing. Don Redman's band would be playing. And he'd just have all those old 78's, you know, just play record after record. And it was a thrill to set up there and listen to all those records, you know.
And that was as far as it went, was the pot.
